reason: The passage depicts Isaac's blessings to Jacob, which are attributed to God's provision and will. The blessings explicitly invoke God's role ('may God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, and plenty of grain and wine') and grant Jacob dominion over peoples and abundance of resources. These material blessings and promises of power would serve to help Jacob and, by extension, the Hebrew people descend from him. The structure of the narrative—where God is invoked as the source of these providential blessings—suggests divine intention to ensure Jacob's (and his people's) prosperity and success. While the passage does not explicitly enumerate Yahweh's abstract goals, the concrete blessings attributed to God's provision demonstrate a pattern of divine beneficence toward Jacob as the ancestor of Israel.
